title: ⭐ Practice: how a tale is put together

questions.prompt: Four readers say what stayed with them after finishing the same novel. Match each remark with the window of the story it is looking through.

options.text: Nothing ever leaves that snowbound farmhouse, and it is all over in three days.
I read faster and faster to find out whether the letter would arrive in time.
The younger sister is my cousin exactly: the same silences, the same temper.
It left me weighing up what a single lie ends by costing the one who tells it.
the plot
the setting
the theme
the characters

questions.explanation: Each reader has answered a different question without being asked it. A house that no one leaves and three days that hold everything answer where and when, which is the place and the moment. Turning the pages to know whether something arrives in time is the run of events and their order, and it is the only remark of the four that could be spoiled by being told the ending. Recognising a cousin in a person on the page is about the people themselves and the ties between them. And what a lie costs the liar is an idea that would survive if the book were reset in another country with other names — the surest test there is for telling that idea apart from the events that carry it.

questions.prompt: A pupil was asked to join two ideas with the pattern of this lesson. He wrote: "There was so a thick fog that the ferry stayed in port." Which line does what he was asked to do?

options.text: The fog was so thick, the ferry stayed in port.
The fog was thick, so the ferry stayed in port.
The fog was such thick that the ferry stayed in port.
The fog was so thick that the ferry stayed in port.

questions.explanation: What the pupil broke is the order: an adjective must stand immediately after so, and his noun group cannot. Rebuild the sentence round the adjective, tie the halves with that, and the pattern is back. Dropping the that leaves a sentence that passes in speech and loses a mark in writing, because nothing now shows which half produced which. Moving so to the middle changes the job of the word entirely: it becomes a plain link between two clauses and stops measuring anything. And such refuses to stand in front of a bare adjective, however natural it may sound to the ear.

questions.prompt: You are taking notes on a sea story, in two columns headed Characters and Action, and you have been told to hunt the main verbs. Which line has earned its place in that table?

options.text: the sea was grey and cold from the very first morning
the captain turned the ship back at the harbour mouth
the ship was forty years old and had been sold twice already
the crew of eleven all wore identical dark blue coats

questions.explanation: Notes of this kind record acts, and an act needs somebody doing something that pushes the story on. Only one line here has a person and a verb of that sort, and turning a ship round changes everything that can happen afterwards. The three others are perfectly true, and all three are in the text, which is exactly why they are dangerous: the weather belongs to the place and the moment, the age of the ship and its two sales are background, and the coats are colour. Take none of them and you have lost nothing; take all of them and the notes are as long as the story.

questions.prompt: A story has reached this point: "Amina had promised the report for Monday. On Sunday evening the only copy was still on the office computer, and the office was locked." Which sentence would carry the story to its climax?

options.text: She reached the building at dawn and found the key gone from its hook.
She had spent three weeks on the report in a small room at the back.
The report was handed in on time and her manager never knew a thing.
Her office was on the second floor of an old grey building near the port.

questions.explanation: A climax is the point at which the pressure is highest and matters must now turn one way or the other. Taking away the last means she had of reaching the copy does exactly that: after it, she either finds another way in or she fails. Three weeks of work in a back room is background and belongs before the trouble started, not at its peak. Handing the report in on time settles everything and would be the resolution, which arrives too early here and leaves the story with no crisis at all. And the floor and the look of the building are the place, which cannot raise tension because it was true before anything went wrong.

questions.prompt: A tale says that the prisoner begged the guard for a blanket. What does that tell you about the way he asked?

options.text: he asked once, politely, and never raised the matter again
he asked for the blanket in return for something he still owned
he asked over and over, in real need, with nothing to offer
he ordered the guard to fetch him a blanket before nightfall

questions.explanation: This verb is not a polite synonym of ask: it carries the anxiety of the person asking and the fact that one asking was not enough. It is the word for someone who has run out of everything else, which is why it fits a prisoner and a guard so exactly. Asking once and letting the matter drop describes a man with other resources. Offering something in return describes a bargain, and a bargain is made between two people who each hold something. And ordering reverses the power between them: a prisoner who could give the guard orders would not need to ask at all.

questions.prompt: A history of a small island prints this line: "That family ruled the island for three generations." What does the sentence tell you the family did?

options.text: they owned every field and every boat on the island
they governed the island and made the laws it lived by
they defended the island against every fleet that came
they measured the island and drew the first map of it

questions.explanation: The verb names power over a people: to govern them and to make the laws they live under. Owning the land is wealth, and wealth is not government — a family may own every field of an island that a governor sent from elsewhere administers. Defending the coast is a soldier's work, and a general who wins every battle still takes his orders from whoever holds the power. Measuring and mapping comes from a different word altogether, the ruler that lies on a desk, and it is the trap this sentence is built to catch.
